plain_english: What's the difference between me, a fool, and you, a wise person? All the difference in the world. Riches are slaves in a wise person's house, but masters in a fool's house. You get used to your wealth and cling to it as if someone promised it would be yours forever. But a wise person thinks most about poverty when surrounded by riches. No general trusts peace so much that he stops preparing for war. War might not come, but it's always been declared. You become arrogant because of your fine house, as if it could never burn down or collapse. Wealth goes to your head as if it were safe from all dangers — as if it were so vast that Fortune herself doesn't have the strength to destroy it.
original_excerpt: "What difference, then, is there between me, who am a fool, and you, who are a wise man?" "All the difference in the world: for riches are slaves in the house of a wise man, but masters in that of a fool. You accustom yourself to them and cling to them as if somebody had promised that they should be yours for ever, but a wise man never thinks so much about poverty as when he is surrounded by riches. No general ever trusts so implicitly in the maintenance of peace as not to make himself ready for a war, which, though it may not actually be waged, has nevertheless been declared; you are rendered over-proud by a fine house, as though it could never be burned or fall down, and your heads are turned by riches as though they were beyond the reach of all dangers and were so great that Fortune has not sufficient strength to swallow them up.

plain_english: You sit around playing with your money and don't see the dangers coming for it. You're like savages under siege who don't understand siege weapons. They watch the enemy building machines in the distance but have no idea what those machines are for. That's exactly what you do. You fall asleep on your wealth and never think about all the disasters circling around you, ready to rob you of everything valuable. But if you take money away from a wise person, you still leave them with everything that truly belongs to them. They live happily in the present and don't fear the future.
original_excerpt: You sit idly playing with your wealth and do not foresee the perils in store for it, as savages generally do when besieged, for, not understanding the use of siege artillery, they look on idly at the labours of the besiegers and do not understand the object of the machines which they are putting together at a distance: and this is exactly what happens to you: you go to sleep over your property, and never reflect how many misfortunes loom menacingly around you on all sides, and soon will plunder you of costly spoils, but if one takes away riches from the wise man, one leaves him still in possession of all that is his: for he lives happy in the present, and without fear for the future.

plain_english: The great Socrates, or anyone else with that kind of strength against life's pressures, would say: 'I have one fixed rule — I won't change how I live just to match your opinions. Go ahead and dump your usual complaints on me from every direction. I won't think you're attacking me. I'll think you're just crying like little babies.' This is what a wise person says. Their mind is free from flaws, so they call out others — not because they hate them, but because they want to help them improve.
original_excerpt: The great Socrates, or any one else who had the same superiority to and power to withstand the things of this life, would say, 'I have no more fixed principle than that of not altering the course of my life to suit your prejudices: you may pour your accustomed talk upon me from all sides: I shall not think that you are abusing me, but that you are merely wailing like poor little babies.' This is what the man will say who possesses wisdom, whose mind, being free from vices, bids him reproach others, not because he hates them, but in order to improve them:

plain_english: and he will add, "Your hatred hurts me — not because it affects me personally, but because it hurts you. When you hate what is good and attack virtue, you're giving up all hope of becoming better yourself. You're not harming me. People don't harm the gods when they tear down their altars either. But your intention is clearly evil, and you want to cause damage even when you can't. I put up with your nonsense the same way Jupiter puts up with the silly stories poets tell about him. One poet gives him wings, another gives him horns. One makes him an adulterer who stays out all night. Another shows him treating the gods badly, or being unfair to people. Some make him a seducer who kidnaps noble young men by force — even his own relatives. Others make him a killer of his own father who steals someone else's kingdom. The only effect of these stories is that people feel less ashamed of their own sins when they think the gods act just as badly."
original_excerpt: and to this he will add, "Your opinion of me affects me with pain, not for my own sake but for yours, because to hate perfection and to assail virtue is in itself a resignation of all hope of doing well. You do me no harm; neither do men harm the gods when they overthrow their altars: but it is clear that your intention is an evil one and that you will wish to do harm even where you are not able. I bear with your prating in the same spirit in which Jupiter, best and greatest, bears with the idle tales of the poets, one of whom represents him with wings, another with horns, another as an adulterer staying out all night, another is dealing harshly with the gods, another as unjust to men, another as the seducer of noble youths whom he carries off by force, and those, too, his own relatives, another as a parricide and the conqueror of another's kingdom, and that his father's. The only result of such tales is that men feel less shame at committing sin if they believe the gods to be guilty of such actions.

plain_english: Even though your behavior doesn't hurt me, I still advise you for your own good: respect virtue. Listen to those who have followed her for a long time. They call out that what they follow is powerful — and grows more powerful each day. Honor virtue as you would honor the gods. Honor her followers as you would honor priests. And whenever someone mentions sacred writings, _favete linguis_ — give us your silence. This phrase doesn't come from 'favor,' as most people think. It commands silence so that religious service can happen without being interrupted by unlucky words. It's even more important that you do this when wisdom speaks to you. Listen carefully and quietly to that oracle.
original_excerpt: But although this conduct of yours does not hurt me, yet, for your own sakes, I advise you, respect virtue: believe those who having long followed her cry aloud that what they follow is a thing of might, and daily appears mightier. Reverence her as you would the gods, and reverence her followers as you would the priests of the gods: and whenever any mention of sacred writings is made, _favete linguis_, favour us with silence: this word is not derived, as most people imagine, from _favour_, but commands silence, that divine service may be performed without being interrupted by any words of evil omen. It is much more necessary that you should be ordered to do this, in order that whenever utterance is made by that oracle, you may listen to it with attention and in silence.

plain_english: Watch what happens when someone shakes a rattle and claims a god told them to do it. Or when someone cuts their arms and shoulders until they bleed, pretending it's religious. Or when someone crawls down the street on their knees, howling. Or when some old man dressed in white robes comes out in broad daylight carrying a lamp and laurel branch, shouting that the gods are angry. You all crowd around these people. You hang on their every word. You convince each other that they must be speaking for the gods.
original_excerpt: Whenever any one beats a sistrum,[6] pretending to do so by divine command, any proficient in grazing his own skin covers his arms and shoulders with blood from light cuts, any one crawls on his knees howling along the street, or any old man clad in linen comes forth in daylight with a lamp and laurel branch and cries out that one of the gods is angry, you crowd round him and listen to his words, and each increases the other's wonderment by declaring him to be divinely inspired.
